mcqs.question: A service passes a load test at expected peak traffic with no issues. Six months after launch, it develops a slow degradation that only appears after roughly 10 hours of continuous operation. What kind of test would have caught this before launch?
options: A second load test run at the same expected peak for the same short duration
A stress test pushing well beyond expected peak load
Running the load test on a larger, more production-like server
A soak test — sustained, moderate load run for many hours, specifically designed to surface degradation that only accumulates over time
mcqs.explanation: Load testing confirms behavior at expected peak over a short window and stress testing finds the ceiling — neither is designed to catch slow accumulation like a leak. A soak test runs realistic, sustained load for hours specifically to surface exactly this class of gradual degradation.

mcqs.question: During a ramping load test, a system's latency stays flat as load increases from 40% to 70% of a candidate ceiling, then breaks sharply upward between 70% and 75%, even though the system doesn't crash until 95%. What is the actionable capacity number here?
options: 95% — the load level where the system actually stops responding
40% — the highest load level confirmed to have zero latency impact
The midpoint between 75% and 95%, as a safety compromise
Roughly 70-75% — the knee, where latency first breaks its target, since real users experience degraded service well before the system technically fails
mcqs.explanation: The knee — where latency first breaks down — is the point past which real users have a bad experience, regardless of whether the system stays technically up until much higher load. Treating the crash point as the capacity number ignores that the SLO was already violated well before that.

mcqs.question: A load test finds the system's ceiling, but CPU utilization at that ceiling is well under 50%. What does this suggest, and what should happen next?
options: The load test itself is invalid, since CPU should always be near 100% at a true ceiling
The system needs more CPU cores, since CPU is clearly the constraint
The ceiling should be reported as-is without further investigation, since a number was found

Low CPU at the ceiling suggests a different resource is the actual bottleneck — a lock, connection pool, or downstream dependency — and that resource needs to be identified before deciding what to scale
mcqs.explanation: A ceiling reached with low CPU utilization is the classic signature of a non-CPU bottleneck — a contended lock, an exhausted connection pool, or a slow downstream call. Adding CPU capacity wouldn't help; the fix has to target whatever resource actually saturated first, which requires further diagnosis, not just accepting the number.

mcqs.question: Why might a service pass both a load test and a stress test cleanly, yet still fail in production due to a capacity-related issue?
options: Load and stress tests are inherently unreliable and cannot be trusted for capacity decisions
The production environment always has different hardware than any test environment

Neither load nor stress testing runs long enough to catch a slow degradation — like a memory leak or a connection leak — that only becomes visible after many hours of sustained operation, which only a soak test would surface
Load and stress tests only measure throughput, never latency, so failures related to latency SLOs are invisible to them
mcqs.explanation: Load and stress tests are typically short — minutes, not hours — so they can't observe a failure mode that only accumulates over sustained operation, such as a slow leak. That gap is specifically what soak testing exists to close, and skipping it leaves exactly this class of production failure uncaught.

mcqs.question: A team wants the most realistic possible validation of a performance-sensitive change before it reaches all users. Why might staging alone be insufficient, and what closes the gap?
options: Staging is always sufficient, since any environment with the same code is equally representative
The gap is closed by simply running the staging test for a longer duration

Staging's synthetic traffic can never fully replicate production's real request shape, skew, and cache behavior, no matter how carefully constructed; shadow or replay testing against real production traffic closes that specific gap
The gap is closed by increasing the staging environment's hardware to match production exactly
mcqs.explanation: Staging's realism is capped by how well its synthetic traffic model matches reality — even careful modeling can miss skew or patterns that only real traffic exhibits. Shadow or replay testing mirrors or replays actual production requests, closing that specific realism gap that no amount of staging refinement fully solves.

mcqs.question: A load test using all-cache-hit, uniformly-sized, zero-think-time synthetic traffic reports a comfortable 3x safety margin over expected peak. In production, the service struggles near expected peak itself. What is the most likely root cause?
options: Production hardware is fundamentally slower than the test environment
The 3x margin was real at the time of testing but degraded due to unrelated code changes shipped afterward
The load-testing tool itself has a bug that overstates throughput

The synthetic traffic never exercised the cache-miss path, real request-size skew, or realistic concurrency implied by actual user think time — so the test measured a system that doesn't correspond to real production load at all
mcqs.explanation: All-cache-hit, uniform, zero-think-time traffic is unrealistic in three compounding ways: it never touches the more expensive cache-miss path, hides the cost of occasional large requests, and misrepresents real concurrency — so the reported margin describes a workload that doesn't resemble production traffic at all, regardless of how confident the number looked.
